newsitem.title: FRANCE: Dassault asks Japan to open fighter market.
newsitem.headline: Dassault asks Japan to open fighter market.

text.p: Dassault Aviation chairman Serge Dassault asked the Japanese Federation of Economic Organisations, the Keidanren, for support on Friday in opening up the Japanese market for fighter planes.
At a luncheon in Paris for Keidanren delegates hosted by the French employers' association CNPF, Dassault asked why Japan bought only U.S. fighters without examining other options.
"From an economic viewpoint you're correct, but from a security standpoint, the most important thing is the reality of our relations with the United States," said Keidanren vice chairman Yutaka Kume.
Kume, who is a counselor at Nissan Motor Co Ltd, stressed that his opinion was personal. "I'm not a representative of the government."

Keidanren chairman Shoichiro Toyoda, who is also chairman of Toyota Motor Corp, added that Japan was the second-biggest buyer of European Airbus Industrie planes after France and had equipped 39 percent of its air fleet with Airbus planes.
Dassault afterwards told Reuters, "We have a good plane -- the Rafale. They prefer to buy American models without even consulting others. That's not normal. There should be competition."
French businessmen also queried the imbalance of the car trade between Europe and Japan.

Nissan's Kume said Japan's carmakers were trying to build on site in the United States and Europe "to contribute to local jobs and local development. We believe the cars built in Europe should be considered European products."

Toyoda said Europe remained a "privileged place for investment" and said a slowdown in Japanese investment in Europe was due to the weakness of the Japanese economic recovery. He said he expected the Japanese economy to grow around three percent this year.
Around 11 percent of Japanese foreign investment goes to Europe, French officials said.

The business leaders discussed some of the problems France and Japan face in common -- the need to increase the flexibility of their economies while preserving their traditions and the need to eliminate rigidities that slow their advance.
"I'm struck by the similarity of the challenges we face," said CNPF chairman Jean Gandois.
The Keidanren delegation is scheduled to meet French President Jacques Chirac next Tuesday.
